278			}
279		}
280		// Delta state is itself a source-change signal. Do this before the git
281		// fingerprint gate so a changed/failed/overflowed export is never stranded
282		// in the short-term overlay waiting for an unrelated commit or restart.
283		if deltaNeedsReconcile && steps.reconcile != nil {
284			if err := steps.reconcile(ctx); err != nil {
285				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] memory reconciliation failed (durable overlay retained): %v\n", err)
286			} else {
287				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] long-term memory reconciliation queued")
288			}
289		}
290		cursor := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
291		// The hosted step pulls teammates' facts as much as it publishes local
292		// ones, so it must run on idle (no-change) ticks too — a machine that only
293		// receives would otherwise never sync. The defer below makes it run on
294		// every exit path from here down, including a failed refresh: a failed
295		// refresh never advances the main cursor, so a machine whose refresh
296		// always fails (e.g. the graph plugin is missing) takes that path on every
297		// tick and would otherwise be starved of the team's facts forever
298		// (COR-2114; a hand-placed call per return had already missed a path
299		// twice). It is token-free and throttled by its own cursor timestamp,
300		// advanced regardless of outcome so a failing hosted endpoint cannot turn
301		// every tick into an egress attempt. The success path still calls it
302		// explicitly BEFORE the agent steps — the `ran` guard makes the deferred
303		// call a no-op then — so the sync never inherits a context cancelled
304		// during a long agent step and burns its throttle window on an attempt
305		// that never happened.
306		factsSyncRan := false
307		runFactsSync := func() {
308			if factsSyncRan {
309				return
310			}
311			factsSyncRan = true
312			now := steps.now().UTC()
313			if steps.factsSync == nil || now.Sub(cursor.LastFactsSyncAt) < hostedSyncMinInterval {
314				return
315			}
316			attempted, err := steps.factsSync(ctx)
317			switch {
318			case err != nil:
319				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] hosted fact sync failed (local brain unaffected): %v\n", err)
320			case attempted:
321				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] hosted fact sync ran")
322			}
323			markFactsSyncAttempt(cursorPath, now)
324		}
325		defer runFactsSync()
326		fp := steps.fingerprint(ctx)
327		changed := fp != cursor.LastFingerprint || cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero()
328		if !changed && !(cursor.PendingSeed && w.seedAgent != "none" || cursor.PendingDistill && w.distill) {
329			fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] no change; nothing to do")
330			return
331		}
332		// Consolidation throttle: the fingerprint includes checkpoint refs, so an
333		// active agent session flips it every turn; without a throttle the heavy
334		// full refresh would run every tick exactly when the machine is busiest.
335		// A failed delta means nothing carried the new work, so the full refresh is
336		// the repair path and must not wait the whole interval (Bugbot PR #78),
337		// but it is throttled too, just on a shorter clock. The delta and the full
338		// refresh contend for the SAME brain write lock, so an unthrottled repair
339		// would fire the heavy path every tick for as long as the delta keeps
340		// failing, contending for the very lock that broke it. watchRepairWait
341		// escalates after one tick and then backs off to the normal cadence. An
342		// overflowed buffer still forces consolidation immediately: recall
343		// completeness is at risk, and a successful consolidation clears the
344		// overlay, so it cannot repeat the way a failing delta can. The first ever
345		// refresh always runs.
346		if changed && w.consolidateEvery > 0 && !cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero() && !bufferFull {
347			wait := w.consolidateEvery
348			state := "short-term memory is current"
349			if !deltaHealthy {
350				wait = watchRepairWait(w, cursor.ConsolidationRepairs)
351				state = fmt.Sprintf("short-term memory failed; repair refresh backing off after %d consecutive repairs", cursor.ConsolidationRepairs)
352			}
353			if since := steps.now().UTC().Sub(cursor.LastRefreshAt); since < wait {
354				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] consolidation deferred (%s since last full refresh; due in %s; %s)\n",
355					since.Round(time.Second), (wait - since).Round(time.Second), state)
356				return
357			}
358		}
359		if changed {
360			if err := steps.refresh(ctx); err != nil {
361				// Refresh failed: do NOT spend tokens on an unrefreshed brain, and do NOT advance the cursor.
362				// The next tick retries the free refresh before attempting pending agent work.
363				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] refresh failed (skipping agent work this tick): %v\n", err)
364				return
365			}
366		}
367		runFactsSync()
368		reserved, reason, err := reserveWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath, fp, w, agentCalls, steps.now().UTC(), !deltaHealthy)
369		if err != nil {
370			fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] cursor update failed (skipping agent work this tick): %v\n", err)
371			return
372		}
373		if changed {
374			fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] refreshed (deterministic, no agent tokens)")
375		}
376	
377		if !w.agentWorkEnabled() {
378			return
379		}
380		if !reserved {
381			fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] agent work skipped: %s\n", reason)
382			return
383		}
384		// Gated token-spending work: agent seed synthesis and/or distill, at most once per --distill-every,
385		// counted against --budget. A transient failure of one step is intentionally best-effort: we still
386		// advance the spend cursor + budget below so a failed step retries on the NEXT interval, not every
387		// tick (and a step that already burned tokens before failing can't be re-run for free).
388		pending := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
389		seedDone, distillDone := false, false
390		seedAttempted := false
391		if w.seedAgent != "none" && pending.PendingSeed {
392			seedAttempted = true
393			if err := steps.seed(ctx); err != nil {
394				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] seed synthesis failed: %v\n", err)
395			} else {
396				seedDone = true
397				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] synthesized seed (agent step; spent tokens)")
398			}
399		}
400		if w.distill && pending.PendingDistill {
401			switch err := steps.distill(ctx); {
402			case errors.Is(err, errDistillPassBusy):
403				// When distill was the only agent step, nothing was spent, so nothing
404				// may be charged. Hand the window
405				// back instead of logging "spent tokens" and going quiet until the
406				// next one — otherwise a watcher installed beside `setup`'s
407				// hours-long backfill loses its first window (and, if the backfill
408				// outlives it, every window) to a pass that never ran.
409				// A seed step attempted immediately before this may already have spent
410				// tokens even when it returned an error, so its reservation must stay.
411				if seedAttempted {
412					fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distill skipped: another pass holds this brain; the spend window remains consumed by seed synthesis")
413				} else {
414					releaseWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath, cursor.LastAgentSpendAt, agentCalls)
415					fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distill skipped: another pass holds this brain; the spend window was NOT consumed")
416				}
417			case errors.Is(err, errDistillDeferred):
418				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distilled capped batch; remaining sessions pending for the next spend window")
419			case err != nil:
420				fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] distill failed: %v\n", err)
421			default:
422				distillDone = true
423				fmt.Fprintln(out, "[watch] distilled facts (agent step; spent tokens)")
424			}
425		}
426		if err := withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath, func() error {
427			current := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
428			// A newer refresh owns its own pending work.
429			if current.LastFingerprint != pending.LastFingerprint || !current.LastRefreshAt.Equal(pending.LastRefreshAt) {
430				return nil
431			}
432			if seedDone {
433				current.PendingSeed = false
434			}
435			if distillDone {
436				current.PendingDistill = false
437			}
438			return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, current)
439		}); err != nil {
440			fmt.Fprintf(out, "[watch] completion cursor update failed: %v\n", err)
441		}
442	}
443	
444	// releaseWatchAgentSpend gives back a window reserved by reserveWatchAgentSpend
445	// when the gated step turned out to do nothing at all. previous is the
446	// LastAgentSpendAt read at the top of this tick, so the cursor lands exactly
447	// where it was; the budget counter is decremented for the same reason. Failures
448	// are deliberately silent: the worst case is the pre-existing behaviour (a
449	// window charged for a no-op), and a watcher must never die on cursor
450	// bookkeeping.
451	func releaseWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath string, previous time.Time, agentCalls *int) {
452		_ = withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath, func() error {
453			cursor := loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
454			cursor.LastAgentSpendAt = previous
455			if *agentCalls > 0 {
456				*agentCalls--
457			}
458			return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
459		})
460	}

467	// watchStepsForRepo builds the per-repo side effects the watch loop drives. refresh is ALWAYS the free
468	// (seed-agent none) deterministic refresh; seed and distill are the gated token steps. Shared by the
469	// single-repo `watch` and the workspace fan-out so both stay token-frugal the same way.
470	func watchStepsForRepo(cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, w watchCommandOptions, repoDir string, now func() time.Time) watchSteps {
471		return watchSteps{
472			now:         now,
473			fingerprint: func(c context.Context) string { return watchFingerprint(c, opts.Runner, repoDir) },
474			delta:       func(c context.Context) (shortTermStats, error) { return watchShortTermDelta(c, cmd, opts, repoDir) },
475			reconcile: func(c context.Context) error {
476				_, warning, err := reconcileMemoryAndLaunch(c, opts, repoDir, "watch")
477				if warning != "" {
478					fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "warning: memory coordinator: %s\n", warning)
479				}
480				return err
481			},
482			refresh: func(c context.Context) error { return watchDeterministicRefresh(c, cmd, opts, repoDir) },
483			seed:    func(c context.Context) error { return watchSeed(c, cmd, opts, w, repoDir) },
484			distill: func(c context.Context) error { return watchDistill(c, cmd, opts, w, repoDir) },
485			factsSync: func(c context.Context) (bool, error) {
486				storage, err := repoStoragePaths(c, opts.Runner, opts.Env, repoDir)
487				if err != nil {
488					return false, err
489				}
490				branch := hostedSyncBranch(c, opts.Runner, repoDir)
491				attempted, err := hostedFactsSyncAndPull(c, cmd.ErrOrStderr(), opts, repoDir, storage, branch)
492				if err != nil {
493					return attempted, err
494				}
495				if branch != distillDefaultBranch {
496					also, err := hostedFactsSyncAndPull(c, cmd.ErrOrStderr(), opts, repoDir, storage, distillDefaultBranch)
497					return attempted || also, err
498				}
499				return attempted, nil
500			},
501			paused: func() bool { return backgroundPaused(opts.Env) },
502		}

530	// watchShouldSpend decides whether the token-spending agent work (seed and/or distill) runs this tick:
531	// only when at least one is enabled AND --distill-every has elapsed since the last agent spend
532	// (cursor-tracked across restarts) AND the --budget cap is not yet reached. This is the structural
533	// token-frugality guarantee — it bounds seed synthesis exactly like distill.
534	func watchShouldSpend(w watchCommandOptions, cursor watchCursor, agentCalls int, now time.Time) (bool, string) {
535		if !w.agentWorkEnabled() {
536			return false, "no agent steps enabled"
537		}
538		if !(cursor.LastAgentSpendAt.IsZero() || now.Sub(cursor.LastAgentSpendAt) >= w.distillEvery) {
539			return false, "--distill-every not elapsed"
540		}
541		if w.budget > 0 && agentCalls >= w.budget {
542			return false, fmt.Sprintf("--budget %d reached", w.budget)
543		}
544		return true, ""
545	}

547	// watchRepairWait is the minimum time between full consolidations while the
548	// short-term delta is failing. It starts at one tick (a transient delta failure
549	// repairs on the very next pass) and doubles per consecutive repair up to the
550	// normal --consolidate-every, so a persistently failing delta degrades to the
551	// ordinary consolidation cadence instead of thrashing the shared brain write
552	// lock on every tick.
553	func watchRepairWait(w watchCommandOptions, repairs int) time.Duration {
554		wait := w.interval
555		if wait <= 0 {
556			wait = time.Minute
557		}
558		if repairs > watchRepairBackoffMax {
559			repairs = watchRepairBackoffMax
560		}
561		for i := 0; i < repairs && wait < w.consolidateEvery; i++ {
562			wait *= 2
563		}
564		if wait > w.consolidateEvery {
565			wait = w.consolidateEvery
566		}
567		return wait
568	}

570	// reserveWatchAgentSpend advances the refresh cursor after a successful full
571	// refresh and decides whether the gated token work may run. repair reports
572	// whether THIS refresh ran early because the short-term delta failed; it drives
573	// the watchRepairWait backoff and is cleared by the first healthy delta.
574	func reserveWatchAgentSpend(cursorPath, fingerprint string, w watchCommandOptions, agentCalls *int, now time.Time, repair bool) (bool, string, error) {
575		var cursor watchCursor
576		var reserved bool
577		var reason string
578		err := withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath, func() error {
579			cursor = loadWatchCursor(cursorPath)
580			changed := fingerprint != cursor.LastFingerprint || cursor.LastRefreshAt.IsZero()
581			if changed {
582				cursor.PendingSeed = cursor.PendingSeed || w.seedAgent != "none"
583				cursor.PendingDistill = cursor.PendingDistill || w.distill
584				cursor.LastFingerprint = fingerprint
585				cursor.LastRefreshAt = now
586				if repair {
587					if cursor.ConsolidationRepairs < watchRepairBackoffMax {
588						cursor.ConsolidationRepairs++
589					}
590				} else {
591					cursor.ConsolidationRepairs = 0
592				}
593			}
594			if !w.agentWorkEnabled() {
595				if changed {
596					return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
597				}
598				return nil
599			}
600			ok, skipReason := watchShouldSpend(w, cursor, *agentCalls, now)
601			if !ok {
602				reason = skipReason
603				if changed {
604					return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
605				}
606				return nil
607			}
608			cursor.LastAgentSpendAt = now
609			*agentCalls++
610			reserved = true
611			return saveWatchCursor(cursorPath, cursor)
612		})
613		return reserved, reason, err
614	}

616	func withWatchCursorLock(cursorPath string, fn func() error) error {
617		root := filepath.Dir(cursorPath)
618		if info, err := os.Lstat(root); err == nil && info.Mode()&os.ModeSymlink != 0 {
619			return fmt.Errorf("watch cursor directory must not be a symlink: %s", root)
620		} else if err != nil && !os.IsNotExist(err) {
621			return err
622		}
623		if err := rejectExistingSymlinkPathComponents(root, brainLockDirName); err != nil {
624			return err
625		}
626		lock, err := acquireFileLock(filepath.Join(root, brainLockDirName, watchCursorLockName), "watch_locked", brainWriteLockTimeout)
627		if err != nil {
628			return err
629		}
630		defer func() { _ = lock.Close() }()
631		return fn()
632	}

634	// watchFingerprint is a token-free change signal: the local checkpoint ref, the fetched (origin)
635	// checkpoint ref, and the worktree HEAD. Including the origin ref means a `git fetch` that brings in
636	// checkpoint activity from elsewhere also triggers a refresh. When all are unchanged since the cursor,
637	// there is nothing new to ingest.
638	func watchFingerprint(ctx context.Context, runner CommandRunner, repoDir string) string {
639		rev := func(ref string) string {
640			if runner == nil {
641				return ""
642			}
643			out, _, err := runner.Run(ctx, repoDir, "git", "rev-parse", "--verify", "--quiet", ref)
644			if err != nil {
645				return ""
646			}
647			return strings.TrimSpace(string(out))
648		}
649		return rev(v1MainRef) + ":" + rev(v1OriginRef) + ":" + rev("HEAD")
650	}

653	// agent ALWAYS "none", then durably reconciles long-term conversation work.
654	// The coordinator owns projection publication, retries, and crash recovery;
655	// watch only nudges it. Agent seed synthesis remains a separate gated step.
656	func watchDeterministicRefresh(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, repoDir string) error {

660	// watchDeterministicRefreshComponents runs the free refresh with explicit failure
661	// policy and an optional outcome observer. Setup chooses best effort; ticks fail fast.
662	//
663	// historyIndex separates the two callers that were previously identical. A
664	// watch TICK passes false: it runs every few minutes, the per-tick delta
665	// already makes new conversations recallable, and the coordinator consolidates
666	// the durable projection on its own schedule. `setup` passes true, because it
667	// is a one-shot onboarding build (the same shape as a manual `refresh`, which
668	// has always defaulted history on) and it ends by telling the user to run
669	// `entire-brain brief`. With history unbuilt that brief silently drops its
670	// transcript half and prints "history index missing" instead — setup's own
671	// recommended next command, answering with a warning about setup's own output.
672	// watchDeterministicRefreshOptions is the free path's refresh configuration,
673	// built here rather than inline so both callers' intent — above all whether the
674	// history projection is built — is readable and testable in one place.
675	func watchDeterministicRefreshOptions(historyIndex bool) refreshCommandOptions {
676		return refreshCommandOptions{
677			outputDir:       defaultExportDir,
678			checkpointLimit: defaultCheckpointLimit,
679			entireBinary:    "entire",
680			graphBinary:     "entire",
681			scope:           exportScopeAll,
682			// A tick must not bypass the durable work ledger: the per-tick delta
683			// already makes new conversations recallable while the coordinator
684			// consolidates asynchronously. A one-shot onboarding build has no next
685			// tick to wait for, so `setup` asks for it explicitly.
686			historyIndex: historyIndex,
687			semantic:     true,
688			seed: seedCommandOptions{
689				includeTests:       true,
690				maxFileBytes:       defaultSeedMaxFileBytes,
691				maxFiles:           defaultSeedMaxFiles,
692				format:             "markdown+json",
693				agent:              "none", // free: deterministic seed only; agent seed is gated via watchSeed
694				agentQuickTimeout:  2 * time.Minute,
695				agentDeepTimeout:   10 * time.Minute,
696				agentTimeoutAction: "keep-quick",
697				agentMaxInputBytes: defaultAgentMaxInput,
698			},
699		}
700	}

702	func watchDeterministicRefreshComponents(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, repoDir string, historyIndex, bestEffort bool, component func(name string, err error)) error {
703		perRepo := opts
704		perRepo.Env.RepoRoot = repoDir
705		refreshOpts := watchDeterministicRefreshOptions(historyIndex)
706		refreshOpts.component = component
707		refreshOpts.bestEffort = bestEffort
708		sub := &cobra.Command{}
709		sub.SetContext(ctx)
710		sub.SetOut(cmd.OutOrStdout())
711		sub.SetErr(cmd.ErrOrStderr())
712		if err := runRefresh(ctx, sub, perRepo, refreshOpts); err != nil {
713			return err
714		}
715		// Deterministic and token-free, like everything else in this step: index any
716		// checkpoint commits that landed since the entity index's high-water mark.
717		// Bounded and failure-silent — a missing `entire graph` provider must never
718		// fail a tick that otherwise refreshed the brain. Under a reporter it is one
719		// more degradable component, so `setup --json`, `status` and `doctor` can
720		// name it instead of losing the reason to a discarded stderr line; with no
721		// reporter the strict watch path keeps its warning and carries on exactly as
722		// before.
723		entityErr := refreshEntityIndexQuietly(ctx, perRepo, repoDir)
724		switch {
725		case component != nil:
726			component(brainComponentEntities, entityErr)
727		case entityErr != nil:
728			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "warning: entity index refresh skipped: %v\n", entityErr)
729		}
730		_, warning, err := reconcileMemoryAndLaunch(ctx, perRepo, repoDir, "watch")
731		if warning != "" {
732			fmt.Fprintf(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "warning: memory coordinator: %s\n", warning)
733		}
734		if component != nil {
735			component(brainComponentMemory, err)
736		}
737		if bestEffort {
738			return nil
739		}
740		return err
741	}

768	// errDistillPassBusy reports that the gated distill did NOTHING because another
769	// process already held the brain's distill pass lock. `distill` itself treats
770	// that as success — someone else is doing the work — but the watcher must not:
771	// it had already reserved the --distill-every window, so a silent success burned
772	// a whole window (24h by default) on a no-op and logged "spent tokens". `setup`
773	// creates that collision by design, spawning an hours-long detached backfill and
774	// installing a watcher that ticks immediately after.
775	var errDistillPassBusy = errors.New("another distill pass holds this brain")
776	
777	// errDistillDeferred retains pending work after a capped successful pass.
778	var errDistillDeferred = errors.New("distill has budget-deferred sessions")

780	func watchDistill(ctx context.Context, cmd *cobra.Command, opts Options, w watchCommandOptions, repoDir string) error {
781		distillOpts := watchDistillOptions(w)
782		busy := false
783		deferred := false
784		distillOpts.onDeferredSessions = func(n int) { deferred = n > 0 }
785		distillOpts.onPassSkipped = func() { busy = true }
786		sub := &cobra.Command{}
787		sub.SetContext(ctx)
788		sub.SetOut(cmd.OutOrStdout())
789		sub.SetErr(cmd.ErrOrStderr())
790		if err := runDistill(ctx, sub, opts, distillOpts, repoDir); err != nil {

On macOS with launchd, the restart would spawn a detached shell that boots the service out and back in again, since bootout would otherwise kill this very process mid-restart; I'm weighing the ordering and exit-code edge cases around that handoff.

If spawn fails, logging and returning nil just lets launchd's KeepAlive retry, which is no worse than the current behavior and self-heals once the verbs update. The ordering matters though — bootout must fire before bootstrap so we never have two instances racing, and since bootout kills the old process first, no extra sleep is needed before spawning the new one.

For the Linux path, the same staleness check applies but the restart action is simply exiting, since systemd handles respawning the new binary. Windows has no supported manager, so staleness detection is gated off entirely and there's no risk from unsupported syscalls.

CLI, detached, newest first, capped at **25 sessions per pass**
  (`--backfill-budget`; `--backfill-budget 0` explicitly means the whole corpus
  in one spend). `--no-backfill` skips it entirely. It is also skipped on its
  own when no agent CLI is available.
- **The watcher is installed as a persistent background service, by default,
  without asking.** On macOS that is a launchd agent with `RunAtLoad` and
  `KeepAlive` loaded through `launchctl load -w`; on Linux a systemd user unit
  with `Restart=always`, enabled with `systemctl --user enable --now`. It
  survives logout and reboot, and its gated distill step calls an agent, so it
  is a **recurring** spend, not a one-off. There is no confirmation prompt
  anywhere in `setup`. What there is, is a pre-flight line — the FIRST thing a
  run that will register a watcher prints, before any work, naming the label,
  the unit path, and both ways out:

  ```
down and proves nothing leaked.

It is safe on a real machine. Every path the binary can write is redirected into
`.trial-setup/`: `HOME`, the four `XDG_*_HOME` directories, the four
`ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR` directories, and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_DIR`. It also sets
`ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_NO_REGISTER=1`, and **both of those last two are needed**:
`ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_DIR` moves the plist / systemd unit *file*, while
`launchctl load -w` and `systemctl --user enable --now` act on your live session
whatever directory the file came from. Set only the directory — as a CI job or a
smoke test naturally would — and a "sandboxed" run still registers a real,
restart-forever agent on the machine. `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_NO_REGISTER` is the
knob that withholds the service-manager call while still writing the unit, so
what *would* have been installed stays inspectable.

The teardown compares `launchctl list` / `systemctl --user` and the user unit
directories against a snapshot taken before the run, so an existing watcher of
your own is never mistaken for a leak. The run spends no agent tokens
(`--no-backfill` throughout, and the watcher is never started).

```sh
TRIAL_DIR=/path/to/scratch scripts/trial-setup.sh   # sandbox somewhere else

content.text:
**COR-2174 fixed and committed** (`42387ea0` on `cor-2174-watch-daemon-wedged`, 9 files, +331/−37).

What changed:

- **Daemon self-restart** (`internal/cli/watch_binary.go`, `workspace.go`): the supervised loop probes its executable every pass (inode + mtime + size) and exits with a clear log line when it was replaced. The probe only runs when the process is the installed service (reuses the stdout-is-the-unit-log identity test), so foreground runs are untouched.
- **Codesigning pin cleared**: before exiting on macOS, the daemon spawns a detached `launchctl bootout → enable → bootstrap` helper — plain exit would hit launchd's pinned cdhash (`OS_REASON_CODESIGNING`). On Linux, exit alone suffices (`Restart=always`).
- **`installDaemon`/`uninstallDaemon`** switched from legacy `unload`/`load -w` to `bootout`/`enable`/`bootstrap`, so a plain `setup` also heals a wedged machine. `enable` covers labels an older build's `unload -w` left disabled.
- **Honest liveness probe**: `launchctl list <label>` exits 0 for a registered-but-dead job, so `daemonRunning` now requires a PID entry. This fixes the "daemon ✓ running while every spawn failed" half of the ticket and makes setup's idempotence check fall through to a reinstall exactly in the wedged state. (This also overlaps COR-2162.)

Validation: full repo test suite passes, new tests cover the probe, the loop exit, and the PID-based liveness; `gofmt -s`/`go vet` clean; windows + linux cross-builds OK. Recorded the launchd LWCR constraint as a Brain fact.

Two caveats:

- The live launchd sequence wasn't exercised end-to-end here (tests use a fake runner); `bootout`+`bootstrap` is the sequence you verified manually in the ticket. Worth watching the first real nightly rollover.
- Residual gap: if the daemon *crashes* after an upgrade but before its next pass, launchd's stale pin still blocks respawn until `setup` runs or next login. Accepted as rare; the upgrade path itself is now self-healing.
- Your global rule says run `oxfmt` before pushing, but it isn't on PATH or referenced in this repo — I ran this repo's actual CI checks instead.

Say the word and I'll open the PR (after pulling latest main), or move on to COR-2153 (retrieval output caps).

gh pr create --base main --title "fix(watch): restart the supervised daemon when its binary is replaced" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Fixes COR-2174.

## Why

The installed watcher outlives the binary it was started from. After a rebuild, the old daemon's writer-path manifest load correctly refuses fields the new build added (`json: unknown field "transcript_storage"`), so every tick fails forever — distill never runs — while `entire brain status` still says `daemon ✓ running`. content.text:
# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

I'm cataloging issues: the helper's output gets discarded since spawnDetached lacks a LogPath, hiding bootout/bootstrap failures—fixing this means passing the daemon log path so errors surface in watch.log. I'm also flagging a potential race between the helper's bootstrap and the daemon's own exit combined with KeepAlive respawn behavior.

Then I'm digging into launchctl flakiness: bootout can return before a job fully unloads, so an immediate bootstrap right after may fail with errors like "Bootstrap failed: 125" or "service already loaded." I'm suggesting hardening this with a small retry loop that attempts bootstrap a few times with short sleeps between tries. I note the helper already calls enable before bootstrap, which is correct, and I'm now questioning what happens during uninstall if bootout is called on a job that was never actually registered.

I'm weighing whether to tolerate "not found" style bootout errors and proceed with disabling and removing the plist, versus risk leaving an orphaned running job if the stop genuinely failed — leaning toward keeping the error check but flagging it as a question. I'm also eyeing the PID-detection heuristic using a substring match, which seems fine in practice but could be made marginally stricter, and now moving on to think about the second-binary scenario.

There's a real limitation: if a dev build writes a new manifest field without the installed daemon binary changing, the wedge can recur since the probe won't fire — deliberately not addressed per the ticket's second fix direction, so I'm flagging it as a known follow-up tied to COR-2162. I also notice a minor ordering issue where the "re-registering" log message prints after spawning the helper instead of before, which could get clobbered if bootout kills the process early, plus some redundant wording worth cleaning up.

Beyond that I'm double-checking smaller details: the test coverage gap for runSupervisedWatch's relaunch path, confirming the GOOS-gating and env var handling in installedDaemonUnitPlan are fine, verifying systemd's daemon-reload behavior is unchanged, and validating the launchctl enable/bootout/bootstrap argument forms all look correct.

I'm also considering edge cases around throttled restart loops if mtimes flap persistently on something like a network volume, and flagging a possible real bug in runSupervisedWatch's handling when watchBinaryChanged returns a probe on the first pass.

There's a narrow race window: the binary probe baselines at probe creation, not at process exec time, so if the binary is replaced in that tiny gap, the watcher could miss the swap until a subsequent replacement — acceptable given the timescale. I also confirm relaunchInstalledDaemon's sentinel-triggered path doesn't depend on any disabling env var the daemon unit doesn't set, so that's fine.

Now I need to run /simplify per the command instructions. The skill both finds and applies simplifications, but in review context I mainly want findings folded into the output rather than unilaterally modifying an open PR's code — still, the command explicitly says to run it, so I'll invoke it and treat any changes as something to surface rather than auto-commit.

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

<result>Four simplification findings (no bugs claimed; all are shape/maintenance):

**1. `/Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/astana/internal/cli/workspace.go:389-397, 421` — `maintain` and `stale` are two parameters carrying one fact ("am I the installed service"), and the signature lets them disagree.**
`stale` is assigned only inside `if maintain != nil`, so in production they are always both nil or both non-nil — but `supervisedWatchLoop` is now a 7-parameter function with two independent nil-checks, and `watch_binary_test.go:72-78` already constructs the combination production never creates (`maintain=nil`, `stale` non-nil). Cost: every future reader has to re-derive the invariant from two call sites, and the loop grows a nil-check per new daemon-only behavior.
Simpler: one optional value — `upkeep *daemonUpkeep{rotate func(); stale func() bool}`, or, since both run back-to-back at the top of the pass, a single `upkeep func() error` that rotates and returns `errWatchBinaryReplaced`. The loop then has one nil-check and one call.

**2. `/Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/astana/internal/cli/watch_binary.go:43-45` — the staleness predicate ORs three signals where two already decide it.**
`os.SameFile` catches the rename-over case, `ModTime` catches the in-place rewrite; a same-inode write that changes `Size()` but leaves mtime byte-identical is not a case any build or installer produces (the test exercises only the first two). Cost: three conditions to reason about whenever someone debugs a spurious restart, and one of them has no test and no scenario behind it.
Simpler: drop the `Size()` clause, or keep size and drop `SameFile` — not all three.

**3. `/Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/astana/internal/cli/watch_binary.go:76` vs `setup_daemon.go:598-611` — the launchd bootout → enable → bootstrap sequence now exists twice, once as `runner.Run` calls and once as a shell string.**
The ordering and the `enable` step are load-bearing and hard-won (COR-2174), and they are restated in a quoted `/bin/sh -c` script with positional `$1/$2/$3` that no test covers. Cost: the next correction to the sequence has to be found and applied in a second, differently-shaped copy.
Simpler: derive both from one place — e.g. a `launchdRegisterCommands(domain, unitPath, label) [][]string` used by `installDaemon` directly and joined into the detached script here — so the verb order lives in a single function.

**4. `/Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/astana/internal/cli/watch_binary.go:67-75` — two identical "re-registration skipped" branches for what is one question: "can I find the installed unit file?"**
`installedDaemonUnitPlan` already returns `(daemonPlan, error)` and does three error-returning lookups; the `os.Stat(plan.UnitPath)` check outside it is a fourth lookup with a duplicated five-line failure arm. Cost: two places to keep the message wording in sync, and a reader has to notice the arms are byte-identical before concluding nothing differs.
Simpler: move the `os.Stat(plan.UnitPath)` into `installedDaemonUnitPlan` (it is part of "resolve the unit the watcher is registered under"), leaving one error branch at the call site.

Lower-signal, not counted: `watchBinaryChanged` (`watch_binary.go:22-29`) is a one-caller wrapper that only does `os.Executable()` before `watchBinaryChangeProbe`; folding the two lines into the caller would remove a name, though it does keep the test seam clean as written.</result>

content.thinking:
Looking at the reuse agent's findings, I'm weighing whether to dedupe the launchctl sequence by factoring the commands into a shared function, and considering swapping the hand-rolled daemon unit plan for the existing brainWatchDaemonPlanFor helper.

A deeper idea stands out: instead of using a shell script for the detached relaunch, I could have the new binary spawn itself with a hidden reinstall command that performs the daemon install under the registration lock, which would solve the locking concern too but requires adding a new hidden CLI flag.

But I realize the daemon itself can't re-register under the lock since bootout would kill it mid-call, and exec-ing the new binary into the same PID doesn't help since bootout still kills that PID. So the detached helper process really is necessary — the pragmatic path is factoring out the launchd registration argv triples into a shared helper that installDaemon can reuse.

For the GOOS invariant, I'll thread goos as a parameter into relaunchInstalledDaemon so the single-read-site rule stays intact while keeping it testable. The lock bypass concern (R3) is narrower than I thought — it's really just about the helper racing against concurrent setup, not a fundamental flaw.

The daemon registration lock can't be held across a shell child since there's no flock(1) on macOS by default, so wrapping the script won't work; I could route through a hidden internal cobra command, but that's scope creep for marginal benefit, so I'll just document the accepted race window and flag it in review as a known, bounded risk rather than engineering it away.

Tracing through the interleavings between setup's bootout/bootstrap and the helper's bootout/bootstrap, every ordering I can think of still ends with exactly one job registered — worst case there's a brief restart or a silent failure on the losing side, but the daemon always ends up running on the new binary, so the race is benign.

For the smaller items: the bytes.Contains check is trivial, I'll just apply it. I'm skipping the idea of collapsing the three install spawns into a shell call since the runner-recorded spawns are load-bearing for tests and shelling out would lose that. For merging the maintain and stale flags into a single upkeep struct, I'm weighing whether reducing the long parameter list of the supervised watch loop is worth the extra indirection.

I'm leaning toward skipping that merge too — log rotation and restart semantics are genuinely independent behaviors, and coupling them into one struct touches eight call sites for little real benefit. Moving to the probe signals, I want to keep SameFile and ModTime and I'm questioning whether Size is safe to drop, since mtime granularity can hide an in-place rewrite that happens within the same second, even on filesystems with nanosecond timestamps.

Thinking through `cp -p` style copies that preserve mtime over the same inode, Size is the only signal that would still catch a content change in that scenario, so it's cheap but not redundant — I'll keep it and note that it's a deliberate belt-and-suspenders choice rather than something to cut just to satisfy the reviewer's complexity concern.

For S4, I'll fold the os.Stat call into the daemon unit plan helper as part of the delegation refactor. I also want the helper to log to the daemon's watch.log so bootout/bootstrap failures are visible, print the "re-registering" line before spawning, and consider adding a small retry loop around bootstrap to handle the bootout→bootstrap teardown race now that logging will make failures observable.

Given the uncertainty around retry complexity, I'll keep it single-shot but logged for now and flag it as a watch-item rather than over-engineering it. I'm still waiting on the altitude agent and the codex adversarial review before finalizing these fixes, so I'll hold off and give a brief status update in the meantime.

<result>Reviewed the full diff plus `brain.go`, `setup_daemon.go`, `setup.go`, `workspace.go`, `setup_spawn.go`.

First, on the two framing questions you asked me to settle:

- **Exit-on-binary-change vs. classifying the "manifest written by a newer build" refresh error — the probe is the right altitude.** `loadBrainManifestForReplace` (brain.go:199-218) is *correctly* strict; the manifest error is a true statement about a writer that cannot round-trip foreign fields. Teaching `supervisedWatchLoop` to special-case that one error would have made the stale daemon invisible again and would have had to be re-done for the next field, flag or on-disk format the old build cannot read. "The process is running a binary that no longer exists" is the actual root condition and the probe names it. No finding.
- **`daemonRunning` requiring a PID entry (setup_daemon.go:517-530) is right altitude too** — it repairs the predicate itself rather than adding a caller-side caveat, and `status`/`setup`/`inspectDaemon` all inherit it.

Findings:

**1. internal/cli/watch_binary.go:76-80 — the detached `/bin/sh` re-registration re-implements `installDaemon`'s launchd sequence outside the lock that exists to serialize exactly this sequence.** The depth is wrong because the shared infrastructure for "change this machine's one registration" is already built and is more than the three verbs: `withDaemonRegistrationLock` (setup_daemon.go:429-461) exists precisely because "interleaving two bootout/bootstrap pairs against one label" makes one of them fail with *service already bootstrapped* — and the file's own comment says two repos registering at once is the ordinary case. The helper takes no lock, so an upgrade-triggered self-restart can land inside a concurrent `setup`'s bootout/bootstrap window and leave the machine with no registered watcher — the failure the lock was introduced to end. It also forks the verb string: `installDaemon` and this shell literal must now stay in sync on ordering (`enable` between bootout and bootstrap), domain construction and future launchd changes, with nothing to catch the drift. Deeper change: spawn the *replaced* binary (it is the new build, at `plan.Spec.Binary`) detached on a hidden re-register subcommand that funnels into `withDaemonRegistrationLock(env, func() error { return installDaemon(ctx, runner, plan) })`. One place knows the verbs and the lock, the unit is re-rendered if the new build's plist drifted (an upgrade is the most likely moment for that), and `relaunchInstalledDaemon` shrinks to "spawn the new binary detached".

The adversarial reviewer flags a potential race condition between the helper process and daemon uninstall: if a user runs uninstall while the helper is re-registering after a binary replacement, the interleaving could leave an orphaned job running with its plist already removed, persisting until logout.

I'm weighing a mitigation: having the helper verify the plist still exists right before calling bootstrap, which would shrink the race window to effectively nothing, especially since launchd actually reads the plist from disk at bootstrap time anyway — meaning a deleted plist would cause bootstrap to fail outright rather than succeed. That makes the orphan scenario require an even tighter sequencing than I first thought: uninstall's bootout and disable, then helper's enable and bootstrap while the plist still exists, then the plist removal — all within the same narrow window.

A simpler, lock-free fix occurs to me: just add a final bootout call in uninstall after the plist removal, acting as a belt-and-suspenders kill for any job that managed to re-register during that window, rather than overengineering checks inside the helper itself.

Now I'm shifting to a separate concern: even with this fix, machines already in a wedged state won't be rescued since their old daemon binary is still running stale code, and I need to check whether my planned environment-propagation changes actually address that.

Running through the setup logic, if the old daemon process is alive but just failing its ticks, `launchctl list` would still report it as Running, causing setup to skip reinstall entirely — so the live-wedged-process case never gets healed, unlike the spawn-failed case which does. To force a reinstall I'm considering bumping the unit material itself, since any rendered change to the plist contents (aside from PATH) would mark it as not-current and trigger a fresh install.

For systemd units I'd need the same trick — adding a revision comment line to the unit file, since the material comparison is just textual. The question is whether this one-time migration is worth it, given the affected population is really just machines currently wedged plus any that wedge between now and adopting this build; after that, the probe takes over for future cases.

Rechecking my daemonRunning fix against the wedged states: state A, daemon alive but ticks failing, still reports Running=true and skips — meaning the old daemon with no probe persists forever since setup just says "already running," the bug surviving its own fix for current victims. A revision bump forces one reinstall everywhere so everyone lands on a probed build — cheap, self-limiting, worth doing. I'll add a benign revision marker key into renderLaunchdPlist.

Instead of an unknown plist key, safer to use an XML comment like unit-revision markers, since plist and systemd parsers both ignore comments but my material-comparison code still includes them in its diff — so a bumped comment triggers drift and a one-time reinstall. I confirm daemonUnitMaterial compares full contents with masked PATH, so the comment change makes it non-Current and runSetupDaemonLocked reinstalls. Now I'm turning to another issue: uninstall failing when the plist exists but the launchd job isn't loaded.

Since bootout failures are brittle to detect across macOS versions by exit code or string matching, I'm writing logic that only treats a bootout failure as fatal if `launchctl list` confirms the job still exists — otherwise it's just absence and should be ignored.

For tests, I'm updating the recording runner to map bootout and list errors separately, keeping the existing stop-failure test passing while adding a new case where both bootout and list fail but uninstall still proceeds to remove the plist. Next I need to tackle C2, the altitude issue, by propagating the daemon environment and passing label/unit path explicitly into the service rather than relying on implicit state.

Propagating the daemon directory through environment fixes the scoped-install path — combined with the stat guard and plist-existence check in bootstrap, a wrong-daemon restart now requires both a scoped daemon and a default plist present, which is an acceptable edge case given DaemonName falls back to default when stale. I also need to reconcile this with the C1 fix, since the helper's enable logic could re-enable during uninstall, but the trailing bootout at the end of uninstall should close that gap. For the bootstrap flake (C5), I'm sketching a bounded retry loop in shell that attempts launchctl bootstrap a few times before giving up.

To keep a single source of truth for these launchctl verbs, I'm defining a shared Go function that returns the ordered sequence of invocations — bootout (ignoring failure), enable (ignoring failure), then bootstrap as the call that must actually succeed.

Writing helper script logic...

A full constant extraction feels overkill, so I'll settle for comments linking the two call sites plus a cheap regression test checking the script's verb order — partial but defensible. I'm also reconsidering the hidden-subcommand approach again since multiple reviewers suggested variants, like a hidden `daemon-reregister` command that runs the lock, plan, and install steps together with logging.

This would fix the lock and logging issues and avoid duplicated shell logic, though it only helps the relaunch path for the new binary, not currently-stuck old daemons. There's a wrinkle: since the exiting daemon spawns the helper using its own binary path, and that binary is already the new build introduced by this PR, the hidden command should exist — but I need to think through what happens during the transition period when an old, pre-PR daemon is the one still running.

Since the old daemon has no probe and never attempts a relaunch, it just gets handled through the normal revision-bump reinstall path, so this new command only ever gets invoked by builds that already know about it, making it safe. entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

git add internal/cli/root.go internal/cli/setup.go internal/cli/setup_daemon.go internal/cli/watch_binary.go internal/cli/watch_binary_test.go internal/cli/testdata/setup_daemon_launchd.plist.golden internal/cli/testdata/setup_daemon_systemd.service.golden && git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix(watch): harden the daemon self-restart found in review

Five review findings against the previous commit, all fixed here:

- The detached re-register helper was a /bin/sh copy of installDaemon's
  launchctl sequence, ran outside the registration lock, discarded its
  output, and re-derived the unit identity from environment the daemon
  does not have. It is now the replaced binary itself running a hidden
  `daemon-reregister` command: one place owns the verbs, the lock is
  held, output lands in the daemon log, and a unit removed by a
  concurrent `setup --uninstall-daemon` is left removed.
- `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_DIR` is carried into the unit's environment, so
  a watcher installed into an overridden unit directory re-registers
  its own unit rather than resolving the default path.
- A rendered unit-revision comment forces one reinstall through the
  next `setup`: a wedged pre-probe daemon is alive, so it reports
  "already running" and would otherwise never be replaced by a build
  that can see its binary change.
- uninstall tolerates a job the service manager no longer lists:
  bootout fails for absence too, and absence is what uninstall wants.
- `daemonRunning` matches the PID entry with bytes.Contains instead of
  copying the whole launchctl payload into a string.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git push 2>&1 | tail -1
